newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures settled slightly lower on Wednesday after trading in a fairly narrow range ahead of a key government policy speech by new Prime Minister Lionel Jospin due on Thursday.

Analysts said the market was cautious about the announcement of measures both designed to appease voters and likely to increase spending but said there probably would not be a huge reaction as the overall state of French public finances would not become clear until later next month.
Traders said, however, as most domestic and non-resident investors were long, any gains would also be limited.

"People are focusing on the Jospin policy speech tomorrow. If anything the market is prepared for the worst although we're unlkely to hear very much new," Yamaichi European economist David Brickman said.

"It would be surprising if he comes out with concrete measures when doesn't know where starting point is. He can say their intention is to shift the burden of tax from labour to capital...but we're unlikely to get the overall fiscal picture," he said.
Jospin was due to give a speech to parliament at 1300 GMT on Thursday, outlining the new government's programme.
Traders said local speculators had tried to push the contract higher in the morning but cut their positions when the it ran into resistance near 129.

A weak start to the U.S. session weighed on the French contract, sending it through key support at 128.74 and down to the day's low of 128.60. However a downward revision to U.S. unit wage costs, coupled with talk of central bank buying, buoyed U.S. bonds which in turn drove core European bonds higher and squeezed out short positions taken earlier in the day.
The French September bond contract settled at 128.86, down 0.08, and little changed from the opening level of 128.82.
Analysts said the key for the French 1997 deficit would be the outcome of an audit of public finances, due by the middle of July, and any measures introduced to offset higher spending.
However French government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said on Wednesday it was unlikely there would be a mini-budget until after the summer break.
"We'll be in limbo until mid-July," Brickman said.

Traders in Paris said the fact most domestic and foreign investors had bought bonds after an agreement on the stability pact was signed in Amsterdam was also limiting the potential of the French bond market to climb.

One trader said the French bond market remained relatively strong and "the only thing limiting the potential of the market to climb is the fact lots of people, domestics and non-residents, are long". He said the contract would probably remain above a gap left between 128.40-44.

One trader said some non-residents had been selling two-year French bonds and buying the short end in Germany on the grounds the narrowing of the spread to 15 basis points on Tuesday was probably overdone and that it was the part of the curve most at risk from domestic shocks.
The spread widened to 17 basis points on Wednesday. The 10-year spread remained steady at minus 13 basis points.

September PIBOR came under pressure along with the long end in the early afternoon, dropping as low as 96.52, but took some comfort from the recovery of the franc against the mark late in the day to settle down one basis point.

The franc fell as low as 3.3762 after a story in the Financial Times repeated reports of government estimates, first released in April, suggesting the 1997 public deficit could be as high as 3.8 percent.
It was trading at 3.3740 per mark at 1545 GMT compared with 3.3721 on Tuesday.
David Clarke, Paris Newsroom +331 4221 5542
